conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility / extractor use and standing rule
dialogue_quality_notes: Agent B repeatedly presses for a specific standing rule (extractor for 10 minutes) across rounds, producing some repetition.
Agent C contributes a concrete constraint (prep-space cost) and conditions consent to moving the rack — adds substantive grounding.
Agent D quickly agrees to a temporary solution (10 minutes tonight), reducing conflict with B but not with A.
Agent A's behavior (promised 10 minutes but later turned extractor off) introduces contradiction between stated commitments and action.
evaluation.final_reason: Although some immediate practical issues were temporarily managed (A ran the extractor and freed the stove; D agreed to run extractor tonight; C required consent for moving the rack), the central normative dispute — whether cooks must accept a standing rule to run the extractor after cooking — remains actively contested and was exacerbated when Agent A turned the extractor off. There was no affirmative settlement of that standing-rule demand nor of extractor operation after Round 6.
position_change_notes: Agent D changed position from not stated to explicitly accepting a 10-minute extractor run for tonight (evidence: Turn 11).
Agent A verbally agreed to keep the extractor on for ten minutes earlier (Turn 1 and Turn 3) but then physically turned it off in Round 6 — behavior reversed.
Agent C consistently insisted on consent before moving the drying rack and offered a conditional one-time move (Turn 6) — position remained stable.
Agent B consistently advocated a standing rule that cooks run the extractor for 10 minutes after cooking across multiple rounds — position remained stable.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A turned on extractor but explicitly refused a standing rule and refused to move laundry; Agent B demanded cooks run extractor and proposed a standing rule — clear opposing positions about responsibility and property.

Agent A removed the dish and freed the stove and affirmed they'd keep the extractor on for ten minutes (practical dispute eased), but Agent A refused to accept a standing rule and Agent B continued to press for one.

Agent C insisted their drying rack must not be moved without consent and offered a conditional one-time move if asked; Agent D promised not to move the rack and began cooking — reduced immediate friction though the standing-rule issue remains.

Agent B asked Agent D to agree to a 10-minute extractor rule and Agent D accepted for tonight — partial agreement with D, but Agent A's refusal of a standing rule still leaves a substantive disagreement.
No new proposals or concessions; extractor remains on and window closed, the standing-rule dispute and laundry-move consent remain unsettled.

Agent A physically turned the extractor off despite earlier promises; Agent B immediately demanded it be turned back on and again pressed for a standing rule — direct contradictory action and renewed clash over responsibility.

substantive_insights: Tension is primarily between public-responsibility norms (B: cooks should manage odour) and property/consent norms (A and C: don't impose on others' belongings).
Practical trade-off: ventilation reduces odour but risks wetting laundry due to rain-facing window — C's consent requirement foregrounds a concrete cost to moving the rack.
Stove access was an immediate practical contention but was resolved quickly when A freed the stove and D took over.
Agent-level resolutions are partial and conditional (D accepted 10 minutes tonight; C will move rack once if asked), which leaves the standing-rule normative conflict open.
